bank: Bank of England · Monetary Authority of Singapore · Bank of Thailand
title: How much liquidity could a synchronised FX trade still tie up?
summary: The technical experiment connected a simulated UK real-time gross settlement system, Thailand’s Project SAN and a non-production version of Singapore’s SGD Testnet. A single operator could settle FX payments against each other across materially different infrastructures and could net batches across all three. The practical result for a bank is conditional. Offsetting trades can reduce the amount it needs to deliver, but the net debit must still be available and may remain locked while another system responds. The experiment demonstrates a way to save liquidity and recover from certain interruptions. It supplies no estimate of savings against a bank’s existing settlement arrangements.

Table 1 and Figure 1 explain how one workflow could span these systems. The Bank of England’s laboratory implemented a cash reservation within its simulated RTGS. Project SAN linked a tokenised payment system to a domestic interoperability layer. The SGD environment used participant-controlled wallets and required authorisation for each movement. To provide a reservation there, the prototype moved funds into a dedicated bank-owned wallet managed by the operator under the bank’s authority. The systems retained their own designs, while adapters handled their different instructions and confirmations. That flexibility came at the cost of additional responsibility over funds in the wallet model.

The order of operations matters when something goes wrong. In bilateral gross settlement, the operator first matches the two instructions and reserves both amounts. If the second reservation fails, the first can be released. Once it issues the first settlement instruction, however, it commits to completing the linked trade. In the outage illustrated in Figure 4, the unaffected leg stays earmarked while the operator waits for the unavailable system, retries settlement and then completes the other leg. A repeated instruction must be recognisable so that recovery does not accidentally create a second transfer. Participants can therefore face delayed access to their cash even when the process ultimately delivers both legs.

Multilateral netting changes both the funding amount and the handling of failures. Each participant needs to deliver its net position within the batch, while the operator has to construct instructions that each connected system can accept. In the experiment it reserved funds system by system in a fixed order. If one participant lacked funds, the operator could release reservations, remove transactions and try a smaller batch. The appendices show why detailed failure information matters. A failure reported against an individual debit lets the operator narrow the problem. A less specific rejection may require removing one small transaction at a time and retrying, delaying other participants’ otherwise valid payments.

The project’s tests covered invalid instructions, insufficient funds, mixed failures and an infrastructure outage. Across those cases, the operator could complete the linked settlement or unwind the reversible stage. Box A identifies an important gap. The tests did not cover non-overlapping settlement hours or the expiry of earmarks. An overnight hold could permit completion when systems reopen while materially extending the time a participant must finance the payment. Common settlement windows are another possibility the authors identify. They also distinguish this technical commitment from the legally binding finality of payments under different national rules. Both issues would need resolving before applying the experimental outcome to a bank’s actual liquidity limits.

questions.question: Which trades would generate enough netting to justify waiting for a batch?
questions.detail: The project shows that a group of payments can settle on net positions. It leaves the size of the gain under actual payment patterns open. A bank choosing which trades to queue needs to compare reduced peak debits with delays, missed deadlines and prefunding. Request anonymised transaction-level simulations from prospective participants, grouped by currency, urgency and settlement window, and compare the peak cash required with bilateral gross settlement.

questions.question: How long can the unaffected currency remain unavailable during an outage?
questions.detail: Figure 4 holds the good leg while the failed system recovers. The experiment excludes cross-day closures and expiring reservations, so it gives a recovery sequence but no upper bound on funding duration. That bound matters for a desk that may need the same currency for another obligation. Seek the operators’ cut-offs, reservation rules and recovery-time test results, including an outage spanning the close in one jurisdiction.

questions.question: How many unrelated payments might be delayed by one unfunded participant?
questions.detail: The technical appendix shows how different levels of error reporting change which trades the operator can remove. The project leaves the resulting distribution of batch delays unmeasured. That distribution matters for deciding whose trades to admit to a liquidity-saving cycle. Ask for timestamped exception logs from a follow-up experiment comparing granular debit-level reporting with batch-level rejection under similar concentrations of trades and liquidity.

limitation: The findings concern non-production environments and the specific failure scenarios tested. The report supplies no production benchmark for funding savings, execution times or failure probabilities.
